rows.en: After we have found the straight path that will lead us to the place where the principles of the halakhot that embrace the whole Oral Torah, according to its divisions, are revealed to our eyes; and after we have made known that a reasoned examination of these principles will show us the quantity of old halakhot from the time before the destruction that are sunk in the branches, and that their total is so great that each and every part of the Oral Torah reached a fitting level of completeness, it is self-evident that there is no need to say much against the opinion (Jost)⚠1 that the statutes of civil law were not completed at all in the generation before the destruction. On the contrary: by our measure and our rule we find that the statutes of civil law stood at that time in a state of completeness on all sides. And so that our words may be believed, we will set out here, by way of example and sample, the principles of the halakhot on the laws of judicial proof, namely: proof by witnesses, the proof of the oath, the proof of the deed, and the proof of presumptive possession (ḥazakah), which have reached us clearly from the time before the destruction of the Temple. Proof by witnesses: testimony in civil cases is not less than two, to impose a money obligation by it; but the witnesses must be known men whose moral way of life is a surety for them that they will testify only the truth (*Antiquities* 4, ch. 8). Therefore they did not hand over testimony to the ignorant (amei ha-arets) nor accept it from them (Pesaḥim 49b). So too one may not accept testimony from one who is suspected of not telling the truth out of fear and dread or out of lightness of mind; therefore the woman and the slave are disqualified from testimony (Shevu'ot 30a; Bava Kamma 88a; *Antiquities*, ibid.). So too they do not accept testimony from one who cannot discern with a reasoned discernment the matters that he saw or knew, and the minor is included in this rule (Sanhedrin 52b), except that in some matters they accepted testimony about what a man saw when he was a minor (Ketubot 28a). Witnesses who are relatives of the litigants, or of each other, are disqualified (Sanhedrin 27b). And the rule in this was: his uncle and his uncle's son and anyone fit to inherit from him, and anyone who is related to him at that time; one who was a relative and became distant is fit (ibid., the first mishnah). Some are disqualified on account of wickedness. In the first rank of these is anyone who transgresses the religion out of greed for money, such as the dice player, the pigeon flier and the lender on interest: in their eyes these were like robbers, who defraud people of their money unlawfully. So too those who gather the produce of the Sabbatical year, who transgress the religion for the sake of money; and after they were compelled by the government to gather the produce of the Sabbatical year, and were under compulsion, they set the rule on the traders in Sabbatical produce. To these they also added one who is suspected of robbery and violence, even if he is not a robber and violent man known with certainty; and they further added the herdsmen, the tax collectors and the customs collectors (ibid. 25a). This last addition dates from the time of the decree that the Romans decreed, that the land of Judea should be like one of their provinces, and they set up tax collectors and customs collectors to collect the tax and the customs (above, ch. 19). Needless to say, a known and notorious robber, violent man and thief are disqualified, for according to their midrash these are stated explicitly in the Torah in the words "a violent witness" [Exodus 23:1]. One is disqualified because his testimony touches himself, and a man does not testify about himself (Ketubot 27b). That an interested party is disqualified from testimony was a settled and known halakhah, and the sages of all the generations spoke of it as of a clear and decided matter (Bava Batra 43b, and in many places). There are also those disqualified because of a defect in their bodily or mental make-up: the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the blind (Bava Batra 128a). A single witness does not stand in a money matter; but Rabban Gamaliel the Elder enacted that he should stand for the testimony about a woman [that her husband died], even though through this a benefit in a money matter also follows, in the collection of the ketubbah (Yevamot 122a). So too a single witness imposes an oath where two impose money (Shevu'ot 40a). This principle served as a foundation for the early heads of the Sanhedrin, and they founded their enactment on it: that a single witness who testifies about a deed that it has been paid, his testimony stands to impose an oath on the holder of the deed (Ketubot 87a, and see Shevu'ot 45a); and they already acted so before the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder (Gittin 34b). A great rule from of old was that a witness does not become a judge (Rosh Hashanah 25b and Makkot 12a), and the sages of the first generation after the destruction speak of it as of a matter long known and decided; without doubt this rule also held for civil cases. So too it was already decided in the house of study of Hillel that an agent does not become a witness (Kiddushin 43a). The witness must testify that he saw or knew the matter of the testimony; but if he testifies from the mouth of another witness from whom he heard it, they do not listen to him (Sanhedrin 29a). From this we can judge that the halakhah "from their mouth and not from their writing" (Yevamot 31b) already existed then, for this is very close to a witness from the mouth of a witness. This is also hinted at in another halakhah that is in any case old: a man writes his testimony on the deed and testifies about it after several years (Tosefta Ketubot ch. 2, and the Bavli there); and it appears from this that his written testimony is of no use unless he himself testifies by his own mouth. At the taking of the testimony the court would warn the witnesses with awe (Sanhedrin 3:7), and examine and question them (4:1) with seven inquiries (5:1); and once their testimony has been examined they cannot retract and say "we are liars"⚠2 (Tosefta ibid. ch. 6, and Yerushalmi Ketubot ch. 2). If they were found to be liars they were called plotting witnesses (edim zomemin), and they do to them as they plotted to do to the litigant. There is no law of plotting until they make the witnesses themselves plotters (Makkot 1:4), and until the verdict is given (1:5), and until both of them are proved plotters (1:6). A litigant may make witnesses who know testimony for him swear that they will come to the court to testify, but only those fit to testify (Shevu'ot 4:1); and most of the conditions of the oath of testimony are settled and fixed halakhot from the time of the Temple. Included in proof by witnesses is proof by a man's own admission; and a great and ancient rule in this is: the admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses (Tosefta Bava Metzi'a ch. 1; Gittin 64a, and in many places). Even witnesses who did not see the deed but testify that the defendant admitted before them that he owes, the defendant is held liable (Sanhedrin 29a); and in this the admission of a litigant is greater than the testimony of witnesses, for testimony of witnesses from the mouth of witnesses is not accepted, but from the mouth of a litigant it is accepted. And even if the admission does not come out of his mouth but is recognizable from his deeds, this is a full admission; this is learned from the halakhot of Admon (Ketubot 109a, 110a). But the admission of a litigant is of no effect in a matter in which he is liable as a fine (Bava Kamma 1:4), for anything that is on account of a fine one does not pay on his own word (Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 1; Bavli 74b). But it appears that this halakhah was not widespread and known, for Rabban Gamaliel the Second, in the first generation after the destruction, did not know of it until R. Joshua reminded him (Bava Kamma, ibid.); and the payments of plotting witnesses, which is certainly a fine, were paid on their own admission until R. Akiva came and taught that they are not paid on their own word (Makkot 2b). The proof of the oath. If there are no witnesses, the oath decides. "All who take an oath prescribed in the Torah take the oath and do not pay" (Shevu'ot 7:1); and these are the ones who take an oath prescribed in the Torah: the four guardians (8:1), one who admits part of the claim (ibid. 6:1; Ketubot 108b), and one who denies everything when a single witness contradicts him (Shevu'ot 40a). Already in an early time they enacted oaths for other matters as well, in all of which the claimant swears and takes, and they called them "great enactments" (ibid. 44b; Ketubot 87); and they enacted several oaths without a claim (Shevu'ot 45a), and these enactments too are old (Ketubot 9:4). In the details of all these oaths we find early halakhot clarifying their conditions (Bava Metzi'a ch. 8 and Shevu'ot ch. 6). The proof of the deed. Writing a deed as security in buying and selling is a very ancient custom; it is found already in Jeremiah, and from the technical terms "the deed of the purchase, the sealed and the open" [Jeremiah 32:11, 14] we learn that the custom of writing deeds was a usual thing from days of old. Deeds of loan too are known in the time of the author of the book of Tobit (4:21), who in any case is not later than the time of Alexander the Great. At first the borrower would write the deed, and afterwards the sages permitted the lender to write it and others to sign; this permission was at the latest in the last half-century before the destruction (Eduyot 2:3). Ketubbah deeds in any case preceded the time of Simeon ben Shetaḥ (Ketubot 82b). They also used to write deeds of betrothal and deeds of tenancy and contracting (Bava Batra 167b), and we find settled and old halakhot on the precise wording of the deed (ibid. 165b), on its form (ibid. 160a), on its conditions (ibid. 167b) and on its validation (Ketubot 18b, 28a); and with bills of divorce Rabban Gamaliel the Elder made an enactment on the signing of the witnesses, so as to make validation easy (Gittin 34b, 37a).⚠3 The deed is strong, in that one collects with it from encumbered property (Bava Batra 175a), but an oath is required (Ketubot 86a). Certainly they wrote a guarantee explicitly, for if he did not write "all my property is pledged" he cannot collect from encumbered property (Bava Metzi'a 13b, according to the Sages), just as Simeon ben Shetaḥ enacted for the ketubbah that the husband should write "all my property is pledged for the ketubbah," for if he did not write so she cannot collect from encumbered property (Ketubot 82b, and see there 56b in Tosafot). With the ketubbah deed in particular they were very exacting, and they did not let anyone sign the ketubbot of women of proper lineage except priests, Levites and Israelites who marry their daughters into the priesthood (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin ch. 1, and Tosefta ch. 7). Remnants of the wording of the ketubbah deed have survived for us: the people of Jerusalem had a special wording, and the people of Galilee did as they did, but the people of Judea not so (Ketubot 52b). A divorced woman could not collect with a ketubbah deed unless there was a bill of divorce with it; and so with a deed of loan, one does not collect after the Sabbatical year unless there is a prozbul with it (Ketubot 89a). Besides these deeds, there were in use at that time deeds for every matter of law and dealings between people, such as wills, gifts, receipts, hypothecs, deeds of valuation, deeds of maintenance, deeds of refusal (mi'un) and deeds of selection of judges; and in the examination of all of them we find halakhot and laws whose origin is from the time of the Temple.{v1_11_08:1} The proof of presumptive possession (ḥazakah). This kind of proof is found in various matters and forms. A presumption: all that is in a man's hand is his, and one who wants to take it from his hand needs proof by witnesses. On this is founded the rule that runs through all civil law, "the one who takes from his fellow bears the burden of proof," and the Tannaim call it a great rule in law (Bava Kamma 46a); and an anonymous Mishnah treats it as a known and accepted premise and says: "for the one who takes from his fellow bears the burden of proof" (Ḥullin 134a; Teharot 4:12). Likewise R. Eliezer, who lived in the days of the Temple and after it, treats this rule as a known premise (Bikkurim 4:10).⚠4 And already the House of Hillel built several halakhot on the foundation of this rule, although they did not mention it explicitly (Ketubot 80b; Sotah 24a; Bava Batra 157a, 158a). There is no number to all the settled halakhot of which it is recognizable and clear, from their content and form and from the way the first sages after the destruction discuss them, that they are old and all rest on this rule. A presumption that comes from reasoned judgment: that is, when there is a doubt whether an act was done in such and such a way, and experience shows that at a certain time or under a particular condition people usually do it, then they relied on this reasoned judgment and held the matter to be done with certainty. On a presumption of this kind many great halakhot in civil law were founded already in an early time. Such is the old halakhah that a woman who comes and says "my husband is dead" is believed if there is peace between him and her and also peace in the world; and this is from their reasoning that a woman does not say "my husband is dead" of one with whom she lives in peace unless she knows for certain that he is dead; and they relied on this presumption also to take out the ketubbah from her husband's property (Yevamot 15:1, 2, 3). So too the halakhah: "[If a woman produced] two ketubbot and one bill of divorce ... she collects only one ketubbah," since one who divorces his wife and takes her back takes her back on the terms of the first ketubbah (Ketubot 9:9); in this they explained that one relies on what experience teaches. Many old halakhot in civil law are founded on this rule (Bava Batra 1:4; 2:6). If we look at most of the laws of buying and selling of houses and movables, on whether, when one sold these or those, some of the things subordinate to them are sold with them or not sold with them, we find that all their principles and their anonymous rules are early, and already the first Tannaim after the destruction discuss them; and the foundation of all of them is experience and reasoned judgment, which went down to the depth of the intention of people who sell an object, what they mean to sell with it (Bava Batra chs. 4 and 5). Close to this is the foundation in civil law of believing the plea of a claimant when he is like one who returns a lost object. Among the early sages it was also called "the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted"; the masters of the Jerusalem Talmud gave it the name "since" (me-aḥar) (Yerushalmi Shevu'ot 6:1 and 7:1), and the Bavli calls it miggo or mi-tokh. Old halakhot are founded on the miggo (Shevu'ot 6:1); and the enactment that one who finds a lost object does not take an oath (Gittin 48b), which in any case cannot be dated later than the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, also had its basis in this reasoning, although they said: "for the sake of the good order of the world." A clear hint of it is found in the words of the sages of the generations of the Temple period, when R. Judah ha-Kohen⚠5 and R. Zechariah ben ha-Katsav testified about a daughter of Israel who was taken as a pledge in Ashkelon, and her family kept her away, and her witnesses testified about her that she had not secluded herself and had not been defiled; and the sages said: "If you believe that she was taken as a pledge, believe that she did not seclude herself and was not defiled" (Ketubot 26b⚠6). By this they hint that it is right to believe that she was not defiled, for only from the mouth of the witnesses who say she was not defiled do we know that she was taken as a pledge. The presumption by which some object is held to be a man's property because it has been in his hand for a known length of time and no one contests it: on this foundation are built great and settled halakhot, and all of them are old. The halakhah on how long the object must be in his hand for him to have presumptive possession of it, and which objects are subject to presumptive possession (Bava Batra 3:1); in which lands they applied this law of presumption (3:2); that the presumption must be founded on a plea (3:3); who are those who have no presumption in an object in their hands (ibid.); which things are not subject to presumption (3:5 and 3:6). Of this kind of presumption various branches are found, and on the foundation of all of them there are old halakhot; but it is not our purpose to go into every detail. Since all the halakhot that have passed before us are clearly old and their origin is from before the time of the Temple's end, as is sometimes made clear from the name of their authors, or from their content and form, and above all from the fact that they are fixed premises for the discussions of the Tannaim of the first generation after the destruction, it is therefore clear to us from these details of the statutes of civil law that this area had already risen to the level of completeness in the days of the Temple. From this area we shall judge all the parts of the Oral Torah, and know that their principles and roots were in full completeness at the end of the days of the Temple. In matters of forbidden foods concerning non-sacred things, the old halakhot are few compared with the great quantity to which this area had already expanded at the end of the first century after the destruction and onward. All the matters on which the Sadducees disputed with the Pharisees concern only matters of impurity and purity, the service in the Temple, the Sabbath and the festivals, capital and civil law; there is not even one matter in their dispute that concerns the forbidden and the permitted in non-sacred things. So too in the whole mass of disputes between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel we find in this area only two or three disputes. And of all the sages named by name who lived before the destruction of the Temple we have only a small remnant on this. So too the old settled halakhot are only a very little compared with the halakhot in the Talmud; but on the whole, the Oral Torah at the end of the days of the Temple was broad and complete in all its aspects.

1.note: Isaak Markus Jost, the historian; the name only is given.

2.note: Read as from בדים, 'lies': 'we are liars'. The printed form is unusual.

3.note: The print reads ל"ז (37a); Rabban Gamaliel's enactment on witnesses' signatures is at Gittin 36a. Kept as printed.

4.note: Bikkurim has only three chapters in standard editions (ch. 4 is an appended baraita). Kept as printed.

5.note: The abbreviation can stand for R. Judah or R. Yose; R. Judah ha-Kohen is the likely reading.

6.note: Printed כ"ו. (26a); the mishnah is Ketubot 2:9, on 27a-b in the Bavli. Kept as printed.

rows.en: However, their work and their great occupation were not only in the practical and halakhic part; they also turned their faces to the part of beliefs and opinions. From the many sayings and the mass of aggadic midrashim that have survived for us from that time we can estimate the completeness of this area. It appears that the effort to widen the bounds of learning in beliefs and opinions was great, for only so can we understand the wonderful sight that we meet in the last century of the days of the Temple. In this century the Jewish religion found lovers among the gentiles, so that many of the peoples of the lands were drawn after them. Little by little it became known among the gentiles that their idols were vanity, and they could no longer find rest for the feelings of their hearts, which longed for something exalted and for a true faith, in the beliefs that their fathers had left them as an inheritance; and a strong longing came upon the good among them to seek the true God, and they found Him in the religion of the Jews. In the land of Adiabene Queen Helena became a Jew, and after some time her son Izates, who reigned in his father's place, also entered the religion of the Jews. In Rome and in Damascus, and likewise in all the places where Greeks lived among the Jews, many of the people of the land became Jews. Without doubt there were many whose hearts were not set on proselytes: Shammai and all who followed him did not want them, and they held that "proselytes are as hard for Israel as a scab." Of many they said that they were only "proselytes of the kings' table," who became Jews only for some other motive, for the sake of power and honor; and even of those who became Jews for the sake of Heaven they said: What use is it if they enter the religion of the Jews, if they know no more than the foundation and do not know its laws and halakhot? And if they learn, who knows whether they will want to learn it according to the teaching of the Pharisees, with all the minutiae of the Oral Torah? Therefore it is better not to accept them and to push them away. But Hillel and his house loved proselytes and strove to bring many into the religion of the Jews, and he paid no heed to all these complaints. For his rule was: even if one becomes a Jew for some other motive, and even if he has learned only the essential foundation of the religion, and even if he does not know how to conduct himself at once according to the whole teaching of the Pharisees, nevertheless, if he wishes to become a Jew with a pure and understanding heart, we accept him, for in the course of time he will become a true Jew. There is no doubt that this is the foundation of the three aggadot that are told of Shammai and Hillel. The first: that a gentile came to them to become a proselyte on condition that they make him high priest. The second: that a gentile wanted them to convert him and teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. The third: that one wanted to become a proselyte on condition that he accept the Written Torah alone and not the Oral Torah (Shabbat 30b, 31a). All three Shammai rejected, and Hillel accepted them. The foundation of these aggadot is to depict Hillel's practice in accepting proselytes: that he did not heed the complaints of Shammai and his house. Even if the proselyte has some other motive, and knows only the essential foundation of the religion, and does not know how to conduct himself as the Pharisees do, nevertheless it is right to accept him and bring him into the religion of the Jews, and in the course of time he will mend everything.{v1_11_10:1} Most of the proselytes were women, but for men the acceptance of the religion was hard because of circumcision. We do not find that at any time they accepted proselytes without circumcision; for how could they bring him into the covenant when he would at once break a commandment laid upon him? That would be like one who immerses with a creeping thing in his hand. Nevertheless, circumcision was not with them an essential without which there is no Judaism. For we see that some of the early sages held that a proselyte who immersed but was not circumcised, for some compelling reason, is a proselyte and is obligated in all the commandments (Yevamot 46b). And the difference of opinion on this already existed at the time when Izates became a Jew: one of the sages of his land taught him the religion of the Jews and told him that he could accept the religion even if he was not circumcised, so as not to arouse thereby the jealousy of his people; for it is possible to worship the true God even while uncircumcised, if only he cleaves to the teaching of the Jews with all his strength. But a sage from Galilee said to him: How long will you neglect circumcision? For it is not enough to know the ways of God and His teachings; one is also bound to keep His commandments, and circumcision is a commandment from which there is no exemption in any way. Had circumcision been considered an essential on which Judaism depends, such a difference of opinion would have been impossible. So too we have seen that in the opinion of some of the sages immersion alone was enough to bring a gentile into the covenant of the religion. Nevertheless they never accepted proselytes without circumcision, and therefore fewer men than women became Jews. Now if we ask what it was that moved the hearts of many of the peoples of the land to become Jews: certainly they did not long to enter the covenant with the Jews because of their worldly success, for the political situation under the Roman oppressor was very bad. Nor can one believe that the multitude of practical commandments and warnings, decrees and fences drew their hearts after them. It can only be that the right beliefs and opinions that they found among the Jews did this. Therefore we say rightly that just as the sages of the generations set their heart on the practical part of the Torah, so they also expounded and inquired into the moral and speculative part, to winnow and purify⚠1 the duties of the heart and the beliefs and opinions that are the foundations of the Jewish religion; and these drew the hearts of the gentiles after them. And in truth the inquiries in these matters, they and their results, reached a high level, as will become clear before us in the following chapters.

1.note: Read as 'to winnow and to purify' (להבר from ברר), as printed.

rows.en: Behold, we have seen that from the day they came up from the exile the heads of the generations and their sages brought a new spirit into the midst of the people. The study of the Torah was their aim and their occupation. The goal of their study was the practical part of the Torah, but the narrative part too was dear to them, to occupy their spirit with it. The ways of study for the two parts were also the same. Just as in the legal part they expounded every single word, and even single letters, to found the halakhot on the words of the Torah, until this way of midrash became a method in the interpretation of the Torah for drawing out new things by it, so they also did in the narrative and speculative part. For every idea born of the intellect they sought a source and a foundation in the Torah. The new opinions that became known to them in the exile and were right in their eyes, and those that became known to them from the Greeks and that they accepted and favored, they strove to find their foundation in the Torah. And conversely, opinions became known to them that they strove to keep away, and for these they sought proofs to refute them. To reach these two aims they used the ways of midrash of the legal part. The view was also spreading that all the narratives of the Torah have a moral purpose; and the first elders proved this from the words of the Torah, "Write this for a memorial in a book" [Exodus 17:14], the meaning in their opinion being that it was to be written in a book so that it might be a memorial for a later generation, to know the measure of the Holy One, blessed be He (above, ch. 12). Philo the Jew goes one step further and wrote that all the words of the Torah and its statutes have a meaning in two aspects, the revealed and the hidden. And without doubt this was also the opinion of the sages of the Land of Israel, as is seen from the way Josephus went in his inquiries into the inner meaning of the Torah and its reasons; he said explicitly that the Torah hinted at several things in wise hints, and in short sayings in the garment of mystery and parable (introduction to the *Antiquities*). From then on they believed that the Torah is the foundation of all wisdom (Ben Sira ch. 24), and that only one who studies it and the writings of the wisdom of Israel and the Prophets will become wise (ch. 39); and this idea filled the hearts of the sages of the Oral Torah. Therefore it is self-evident that for every matter of wisdom and every opinion in beliefs that they held in the course of the ages they were compelled to give a foundation in the Scriptures; and this caused them to act in this part of the midrash of Scripture as in the midrash of halakhah. Therefore in this part too only a minority of the midrashim lean to the plain meaning of Scripture, for most of them strive to show a source for ideas, virtues, beliefs and opinions: whether what they received from their predecessors, or what became known to them from other nations and was right in their eyes, or what they invented from their own minds; to all these they gave a source in Scripture. Many of these midrashim are strange, and in truth some of them have only the value of rhetoric. This is so with midrashim whose basis is a passing cause, and when the cause passes the effect passes too (Zunz, *G[ottesdienstliche] V[orträge]*, p. 58); and likewise, when they wished to rouse the heart of the multitude to some matter, or to speak in praise of certain people or a matter or one of the nations, or on the contrary when they spoke in disparagement and warning, they used the Scriptures by way of rhetoric (Jellinek, *Nofet Tsufim*). But it is not so with the general midrashim, in which the idea placed in them was true for them in itself: in those midrashim most of them had for them the true meaning of Scripture, especially since they held that Scripture has a hidden and a revealed interpretation. All the expositions of this part of the Torah were called "midrashei aggadah." If at times the exposition is strange in our eyes, this is no proof that in their opinion it was not the plain interpretation; for what the ancients called peshat, as against derash, is also strange (Kiddushin 80b; Ketubot 111b; Ḥullin 6a, 133b; Arakhin 8b). Therefore most of the general aggadic midrashim go by the way of peshat, that is, what was called by them the plain meaning of Scripture. These general aggadic midrashim were called "praiseworthy aggadot that are heard in the ears of every man" (Mekhilta, Va-yassa ch. 1). Only very few of the aggadic midrashim and of aggadic sayings in general have reached us in the names of the sages who lived in the early time; but this is no proof that they did not exist. We have general aggadic sayings without the names of those who said them, and sometimes transmitted by sages after the destruction, of which it is recognizable from their content that they are early; and especially we find sayings and ideas in other books from an early time that bear witness to several aggadic sayings in the books of the Oral Torah, proving that they are old.

footnotes.en: See Bava Metzi'a (18b, 21a) and Bava Batra (133b), in the incident of Jonathan ben Uzziel, and in the Mishnah, and there (135a); and in the Tosefta, Bava Metzi'a ch. 1 and Bava Batra ch. 8.
I heard these words, in explanation of the three aggadot told of Hillel, from R. Aaron Jellinek in his sermons in our house of study; and the words are excellent and worthy of the one who said them.
